source.title: Requential Coding: Pushing the Limits of Model Compression with Self-Generated Training Data
source.authors: Shi-Kai Qiu; Marc Finzi; Yujia Zheng; Kun Zhang; Andrew Gordon Wilson

record.file_problem: none; the full paper and appendices are present
record.tranche_reason: The paper measures test loss across model sizes, bearing on the scaling claim, but uses that result in a study of requential coding rather than reproducing the original scaling-law fitting procedure.
record.gate_note: The paper reports a test-loss decrease as model size grows, but does not fit a power law to held-out loss or test whether small-run fits predict larger runs. Its power-law fit concerns requential code length per parameter, not loss. It also uses D=20N as a compute-optimal protocol without testing whether that allocation is loss-minimising.
record.test_reason: The paper introduces requential coding, a model-compression method, and reports code lengths and PAC-Bayes bounds. It uses D=20N as a given compute-optimal protocol, citing Hoffmann et al. It trains GPT-2-style models of varying width but never fits or tests a held-out-loss power law, extrapolation, allocation, shape, transfer or downstream predictability. Test-loss curves appear only as reference lines in the bound figures, with no fit and no stated values. The one power-law fit is code length per parameter versus N, which is a different construct.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that requential coding compresses models far below prequential and PTQ codes, and that larger models and ensembles are more compressible at fixed loss. It gives state-of-the-art PAC-Bayes bounds that tighten with scale under D=20N, because code length per parameter decays as a power law in N. It predicts overfitting under data repetition and separates learnable from random information in datasets. The authors make no new claim about held-out-loss power laws.
record.recipe_differences: The study measures requential code length and generalization bounds, rather than fitting scaling laws to held-out loss or testing the original extrapolation procedure.

fits_no_version.finding: Under compute-optimal training (D=20N), requential code length per parameter decays as a power law in N. Fitted to the five largest models, the exponents are about N^-0.46 and N^-0.15 on CIFAR-5M and FineWeb (Figure 7 right; which exponent belongs to which dataset is not legible in the text). The certified generalization gap shrinks with scale.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Compressed model size per parameter (model complexity relative to data) falls as a power law in model size under compute-optimal scaling, so generalization gaps vanish with scale.

fits_no_version.finding: At fixed loss, larger models and larger ensembles need fewer requential-code bits despite having more parameters (Figures 5 and 6).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sample efficiency of larger models translates into greater compressibility at fixed loss.

record.problems: For the loss-scaling result, the paper gives an endpoint decrease in the Figure 12 caption but no uncertainty estimates or fit of a power law to held-out loss. The other power-law fit in the paper is for code length per parameter, not loss.

untested.parts: No power-law fit of held-out loss to parameters, tokens or compute. Test loss is plotted only as a reference curve in Figures 7 and 12.
D=20N is adopted from Hoffmann et al. as a protocol; the allocation is not tested.
Depth is fixed at 8 blocks and only width varies; no shape comparison at fixed N.
CIFAR-5M image models and multi-epoch training appear, but no loss power law is fitted in those settings.
No fitting-choice sensitivity analysis of loss laws.

record.verdict_notes: The record over-reads the study as testing V1. The study uses Chinchilla's D=20N as an assumed protocol and reports only bound and code-length scaling. Row r1 misattributes bound values to test loss. No verdicts are issued.

versions.untested_parts: The paper reports a test-loss decrease with model size for OpenWebText at fixed data, but does not establish a power-law form, test scaling with tokens or compute, or show that the law holds over several orders of magnitude.
No small-run fits are used to predict larger-run losses.
D=20N is used as a compute-optimal evaluation protocol; the paper does not optimize the parameter/token split or compare allocation trends.
The experiments use a GPT-2 architecture with 8 transformer blocks and vary width; they do not compare depth or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
The paper includes image data and discusses repeated-data training, but does not test whether the same loss power law holds in other modalities or training regimes.
No downstream-task performance is evaluated or predicted.
No fitting-choice sensitivity or departures from a power law in held-out loss are tested; the power-law fit reported is for code length per parameter.

rows.subject: GPT-2
rows.operation_detail: Scaled model size at fixed data and measured test loss.
rows.note: The caption reports a decrease across this size range. It does not report a fitted loss exponent or establish a power-law curve.
rows.check: The 1.51→1.38 nats values in the Figure 12 caption describe the requential generalization bound, not test loss. The caption reads 'The requential bound improves with scale… falling from 1.51 to 1.38 nats'. Even read as loss, this is a two-endpoint decrease at fixed width-only scaling with no fit, so it cannot show V1's power-law form. The row is mis-specified and should be relabelled as a bound measure or dropped.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.reason: Test loss decreases from 1.51 to 1.38 nats, but this result does not establish the claimed power-law form or its broader range; row r1.
